We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{1}{2}^{x}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{1}{2}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{{2}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}]}_{a}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[{2}^{x}]}_{a}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }({2}^{1}-{2}^{a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot (2-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{2}^{a})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y={2}^{x}$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }{2}^{x}=0$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{2}^{x}=\infty $

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14037234/assets/b9a29cbd8a029e0f26e3da6a042ada0f8a809053233979bb4ff73db3dcf0f10d.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{1}{2}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot (2-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{2}^{a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}\cdot (2-0) \\  & =\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)}.\end{aligned}
$$
